column1: What does customer centricity mean in product development?
column2: Make customer needs and outcomes central to decisions.
column3: Teams learn directly from customers rather than relying only on internal assumptions.

column1: What is the goal of Design Thinking?
column2: Understand customer problems and explore useful solutions.
column3: It combines empathy, experimentation, and learning.

column1: What is the purpose of a persona in product discovery?
column2: Represent a type of customer or user and their needs.
column3: A persona helps a team discuss needs in context rather than treating all users as identical.

column1: What is the difference between a feature and a story in SAFe?
column2: A feature describes solution behavior that delivers value. A story is a smaller piece of work a team can implement.
column3: Features are commonly split into stories for team execution.

column1: What is an acceptance criterion for a feature or story?
column2: A condition that must be met for the work to be accepted.
column3: Clear criteria help stakeholders and teams agree on expected behavior.

column1: What is the purpose of the ART Backlog?
column2: Hold and prioritize work for the Agile Release Train.
column3: The backlog helps teams select work that supports the ART vision and goals.

column1: Who has primary responsibility for defining and prioritizing the ART Backlog?
column2: Product Management.
column3: Product Management works with customers, Business Owners, teams, and other stakeholders.

column1: What does Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF) help teams decide?
column2: The order in which to do jobs for economic benefit.
column3: WSJF considers the cost of waiting as well as job duration or a size proxy.

column1: How is WSJF calculated in SAFe?
column2: Relative Cost of Delay divided by relative job duration.
column3: When duration is difficult to estimate, relative job size is often used as a proxy.

column1: Two jobs have equal estimated duration. Job A has a Cost of Delay of 20 and Job B has a Cost of Delay of 8. Which has the higher WSJF?
column2: Job A.
column3: With the same denominator, the larger Cost of Delay gives Job A the higher WSJF.

column1: A job has relative Cost of Delay 24 and relative job size 6. What is its WSJF using size as a proxy?
column3: Divide 24 by 6. Use consistent relative estimates when comparing jobs.

column1: What three factors contribute to relative Cost of Delay in SAFe WSJF?
column2: User and business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement.
column3: These factors make the cost of waiting visible when comparing work.

column1: What is a Planning Interval (PI) in current SAFe terminology?
column2: A cadence-based timebox in which an ART delivers value in alignment with PI objectives.
column3: A PI typically lasts 8 to 12 weeks and contains multiple iterations.

column1: What is the main purpose of PI Planning?
column2: Align the ART and stakeholders on a shared mission and plan for the upcoming PI.
column3: Teams coordinate work, identify dependencies, and create PI objectives.

column1: Who facilitates PI Planning for the ART?
column2: The Release Train Engineer (RTE).
column3: The RTE helps the train coordinate and supports effective events.

column1: Who plans the team-level work during PI Planning?
column2: The Agile Teams that will do the work.
column3: Teams collaborate with stakeholders and other teams to create a feasible plan.

column1: Why do teams identify dependencies during PI Planning?
column2: Dependencies show where one team's work affects another team's work.
column3: Making dependencies visible allows teams to coordinate and reduce delivery risk.

column1: What do team PI objectives describe?
column2: The business and technical goals a team intends to achieve in the PI.
column3: Objectives communicate intended outcomes rather than listing every task.

column1: Who assigns planned business value to team PI objectives during planning?
column2: Business Owners.
column3: Business Owners discuss the objectives with teams and help clarify their relative business value.

column1: What is an uncommitted PI objective?
column2: An objective that the team plans but does not commit to achieving.
column3: It helps make uncertain or lower-confidence work visible without treating it as a commitment.

column1: What is the purpose of the confidence vote at PI Planning?
column2: Assess whether participants believe the plan is achievable.
column3: Low confidence signals that the plan or unresolved risks need more discussion.

column1: What does ROAM help participants do with PI risks?
column2: Classify risks as resolved, owned, accepted, or mitigated.
column3: The classification makes it clear how the ART will handle each risk.

column1: What is the purpose of a team breakout during PI Planning?
column2: Let teams plan their work, objectives, and dependencies with relevant stakeholders.
column3: Teams refine the plan as they learn about capacity and cross-team needs.

column1: What is the purpose of the ART planning board?
column2: Visualize planned features, milestones, and dependencies across teams.
column3: The shared view exposes coordination issues during and after planning.

column1: Why should a team consider capacity during PI Planning?
column2: The plan must fit the people and time available.
column3: Ignoring capacity increases the risk of overcommitment.

column1: What is the role of the System Demo during a PI?
column2: Show the integrated work of the ART and gather feedback.
column3: Demonstrating the integrated solution reveals issues that separate team demos can miss.

column1: What does Inspect and Adapt accomplish at the end of a PI?
column2: It reviews the solution and performance, then identifies improvements.
column3: The event includes a PI System Demo, measurement review, and problem-solving workshop.

column1: What is the purpose of the Innovation and Planning iteration?
column2: Provide time for activities such as innovation, planning, and improvement.
column3: It helps make space for these activities instead of treating every iteration as feature delivery.

column1: What should an ART do when feedback shows a feature does not solve the customer's problem?
column2: Use the evidence to adjust the solution or change direction.
column3: Delivering a planned feature is not the same as achieving a useful outcome.

column1: Why is limiting work in process useful during PI execution?
column2: It helps teams finish current work and exposes bottlenecks.
column3: Starting many features at once can increase waiting and slow feedback.

column1: What is the purpose of an iteration review?
column2: Show completed team work and collect stakeholder feedback.
column3: Feedback helps the team adjust future work.

column1: What is the purpose of an iteration retrospective?
column2: Identify ways for the team to improve how it works.
column3: The team selects actionable improvements based on its experience.
